overview: Plantar fibromatosis, also called Ledderhose disease, is a benign condition in which firm, slow-growing nodules form within the plantar fascia, the band of tissue under the arch. The nodules are not cancerous and do not spread, but they can become painful when they are pressed by body weight and shoes. The course is unpredictable: some lumps stay stable for years, others slowly enlarge.
pathophysiology: Fibroblasts in the plantar fascia multiply and lay down excess collagen, forming dense nodules or thickened cords, most often in the central or inner part of the fascia. The cause is not fully understood. It is related to Dupuytren contracture of the hand, and the two conditions often occur together.
symptoms: One or more firm lumps felt in the arch of the sole, usually on the inner or central side
Lumps that grow slowly over months or years
Pain or a feeling of pressure when standing or walking, especially barefoot or in firm shoes
A lump that feels fixed to the deeper tissue and does not move freely
Both feet affected in a sizeable minority of people
Toe curling is uncommon, unlike the hand condition
causes: The exact cause is unknown
An inherited tendency, as it often runs in families
Overgrowth of fibrous tissue in the plantar fascia
Possible link with earlier injury or repeated pressure on the sole
risk_factors: Male sex and middle or older age
Heavy alcohol use or liver disease
Long-term use of some anti-seizure medicines
diagnosis: Diagnosis is mostly clinical: the examiner finds firm nodules in the sole that are fixed to the fascia. Ultrasound or MRI can confirm the location and size when the picture is unclear. A biopsy is kept for lumps that grow quickly or look unusual, to rule out a malignant soft tissue tumour.
differential_diagnosis: Soft tissue sarcoma, which is rare
Fibroma or other benign soft tissue tumour
treatment: Watchful waiting when the lumps cause little trouble
Shoes with plenty of room and a cushioned sole
Soft insoles with a relief cut-out under the nodule to reduce pressure
Calf and foot stretching and physiotherapy for comfort
Corticosteroid injection into the nodule in selected painful cases, given by a specialist
Shockwave therapy or low-dose radiotherapy considered by specialists in persistent cases
Surgery only as a last resort, because the lumps often return and healing of the sole can be difficult
when_to_see_a_doctor: See a healthcare professional for any new lump in the sole, and sooner if it grows quickly, bleeds, breaks the skin or becomes very painful. People with diabetes should have any lump or sore on the foot checked promptly.

overview: Freiberg disease is a condition in which the rounded end of a metatarsal bone, most often the second, loses part of its blood supply and the joint surface becomes flattened and damaged. It usually appears in adolescence and early adulthood, more often in girls and young women, and is frequently linked to sport. The pain is felt in the ball of the foot, at the joint at the base of the affected toe.
pathophysiology: The growing end of the metatarsal is relatively fragile and has a limited blood supply. Repeated stress, especially on the longer second metatarsal during push-off, can interrupt this supply, so the bone beneath the joint cartilage weakens and collapses. Over time the joint can become stiff and develop arthritis.
symptoms: Pain in the ball of the foot at the base of the second toe, sometimes the third
Pain that increases with weight bearing, running, jumping or pushing off
Swelling and tenderness over the affected joint
Stiffness and reduced movement of the toe joint
A limp or a tendency to walk on the outer edge of the foot
Sometimes a grinding feeling when the toe is moved
causes: Repeated stress on the head of the second metatarsal
A reduced blood supply to the growing end of the bone
A second metatarsal that is longer than its neighbours
A single injury to the joint in some cases
risk_factors: A previous injury to the forefoot
diagnosis: A clinician examines the joint for tenderness, swelling and limited movement. X-rays can look normal early on; later they show a flattened, dense or fragmented metatarsal head and widening of the joint space. MRI can detect changes sooner and shows how much bone is affected.
differential_diagnosis: Synovitis or capsulitis of the toe joint
treatment: Relative rest and avoiding the activities that cause pain
A stiff-soled shoe, rocker-sole shoe or walking boot to offload the forefoot
A metatarsal pad or custom orthoses to redistribute pressure
Short-term immobilisation in a cast or boot in more painful cases
Pain relief medicines only if suitable for the person, as advised by a pharmacist or doctor
Physiotherapy to keep the joint moving as symptoms settle
Surgery for persistent pain or advanced joint damage, for example removing loose bone or reshaping the bone
when_to_see_a_doctor: See a healthcare professional if forefoot pain at the base of a toe lasts more than a couple of weeks, especially in a growing young person who plays sport, or if the toe becomes stiff or swollen. Seek urgent care for severe pain after an injury, or redness, warmth and fever.

overview: Plantar nerve compression happens when a nerve running to the toes is squeezed in the front part of the sole. The most common form is Morton neuroma, a thickening of tissue around a nerve between two metatarsal heads, usually between the third and fourth toes. It causes burning pain in the ball of the foot and tingling in the toes, often provoked by tight shoes.
pathophysiology: A common plantar digital nerve passes under the ligament that links the metatarsal heads. Repeated pinching of the nerve, particularly when the forefoot is squeezed or the toes are forced upward, irritates it and leads to scarring and thickening of the surrounding tissue. The enlarged nerve then becomes more sensitive to pressure.
symptoms: Burning or sharp pain in the ball of the foot, often spreading into two neighbouring toes
Tingling or numbness between the toes
A feeling of standing on a pebble or on a folded sock
Pain that is worse in narrow or high-heeled shoes
Relief when the shoe is removed and the forefoot is massaged
Pain that increases with walking, running or standing on tiptoe
causes: Tight, narrow or pointed shoes that squeeze the forefoot
High heels that push weight onto the ball of the foot
Repeated forefoot pressure from running or jumping sports
Foot deformities such as bunions, hammer toes, flat feet or high arches
Previous injury or scarring in the forefoot
risk_factors: Female sex, with a peak between about 40 and 60 years
Regular use of high heels or narrow shoes
Work that involves kneeling or squatting on the toes
diagnosis: Diagnosis is mainly clinical. Pressing the space between the metatarsal heads, or squeezing the forefoot from the sides, reproduces the pain, and a click may be felt. Ultrasound or MRI can show the thickened nerve and help exclude other causes. Nerve tests are sometimes used when numbness is widespread.
differential_diagnosis: Inflammation of the toe joint at the base of a toe
Peripheral neuropathy, for example from diabetes
Nerve root irritation from the lower back
treatment: Wider shoes with a roomy toe box and a low heel
A metatarsal pad placed just behind the painful area to spread the metatarsal heads
Custom or off-the-shelf orthoses to reduce forefoot pressure
Reducing activities that provoke the pain for a time
Pain relief medicines only if suitable for the person, as advised by a pharmacist or doctor
Corticosteroid or other injections given by a specialist when simple measures fail
Surgery to release the pressure or remove the nerve segment if symptoms persist, with permanent numbness between the toes as an expected result of removal
when_to_see_a_doctor: See a healthcare professional if burning pain or numbness in the forefoot lasts more than a few weeks, if it is waking you at night, or if both feet and several toes are affected. Seek urgent care for sudden severe pain with swelling, redness and fever.

overview: Posterior tibial tendinosis is wear and degeneration of the tendon that runs behind the inner ankle bone and holds up the arch of the foot. As the tendon weakens, the arch can gradually flatten and the heel tilts outward, which is why it is also called adult-acquired flatfoot. It is most common in middle-aged and older adults, particularly women.
pathophysiology: The posterior tibial tendon works against the pull of other muscles to keep the arch raised during walking. Repeated load, poor blood supply in part of the tendon and often excess body weight lead to degeneration, thickening and tearing. As the tendon fails, nearby ligaments stretch and the foot progressively flattens.
symptoms: Pain and swelling along the inner side of the ankle, behind and below the bony bump
Pain that worsens with walking, standing for long periods or on uneven ground
A gradually flattening arch
The heel tilting outward when seen from behind, with more toes visible on the outer side
Difficulty or inability to rise onto the toes on one foot
In later stages, pain on the outer side of the ankle
causes: Long-term overload of the tendon from standing or walking
Age-related degeneration
Excess body weight
Previous injury to the inner ankle
Inflammatory joint disease
risk_factors: Previous steroid injections near the tendon
diagnosis: A clinician checks the shape of the foot while standing, tests whether a single-leg heel rise is possible, and presses along the tendon. Weight-bearing X-rays show the arch and alignment. Ultrasound or MRI shows the condition of the tendon and whether it is torn.
differential_diagnosis: Arthritis of the ankle or hindfoot joints
Stress fracture of a bone on the inner side of the foot
Other tendon problems around the ankle
treatment: Rest and reduced weight-bearing during painful flares, sometimes with a walking boot
Supportive shoes with a firm sole
Arch supports or custom orthoses, and sometimes an ankle brace
Physiotherapy with calf stretching and strengthening of the muscles around the ankle
Weight management when relevant
Pain relief medicines only if suitable for the person, as advised by a pharmacist or doctor
Steroid injection around the tendon is generally avoided because it can weaken it
Surgery in advanced or non-responding cases, to repair the tendon or realign the foot
when_to_see_a_doctor: See a healthcare professional if you have pain along the inner ankle that lasts more than a couple of weeks, if one arch is visibly flattening, or if you cannot rise onto your toes on one foot. Treatment is more effective when started early.

overview: Metatarsophalangeal joint pain is pain in the joint where a toe meets the long bone of the forefoot, at the ball of the foot. It can come from irritation of the joint lining, damage to the supporting plantar plate, arthritis or overload. The second joint is the most commonly affected. Pain usually increases when pushing off during walking or running.
pathophysiology: These joints take a large share of body weight when the heel lifts. The plantar plate, a thick pad under the joint, and the joint capsule stabilise the toe. Repeated overload can inflame the joint lining or weaken and tear the plantar plate, so the toe becomes unstable and may drift out of line. Other causes include inflammatory arthritis, gout and wear of the cartilage.
symptoms: Pain and tenderness at the base of one or more toes, on the underside of the ball of the foot
Swelling around the joint
Pain that increases when pushing off, standing on tiptoe or wearing flat thin-soled shoes
A feeling of walking on a pebble
Stiffness of the joint
A toe that drifts upward or sideways, or lies crossed over its neighbour
causes: Overload of the forefoot from sport or long periods of standing
Plantar plate strain or tear
A long second metatarsal or an unstable foot structure
Joint inflammation from conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis or gout
Joint wear (osteoarthritis), including a stiff big toe joint
Footwear with high heels or a thin, flexible sole
risk_factors: Bunions, hammer toes or other deformities
diagnosis: The clinician locates the pain with firm pressure on the joint and checks for instability by gently moving the toe up and down. X-rays show joint wear or alignment problems. Ultrasound or MRI can show plantar plate damage or joint inflammation. Blood tests are used when an inflammatory condition or gout is suspected.
treatment: Reducing the activities that provoke the pain for a time
Shoes with a stiff or rocker sole and a roomy toe box
A metatarsal pad or custom orthoses to offload the joint
Taping the toe to hold it in a better position
Ice and, if suitable for the person, pain relief medicines as advised by a pharmacist or doctor
Treating the underlying condition, for example gout or rheumatoid arthritis
Injections are used with caution because they can weaken the plantar plate
Surgery for persistent instability, deformity or advanced arthritis
when_to_see_a_doctor: See a healthcare professional if pain at the base of a toe lasts more than a few weeks, if the toe is changing position, or if several joints are painful and swollen. Seek urgent care for a hot, red, very swollen joint, especially with fever, or for sudden severe pain after an injury.
